messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 28
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Tailor
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Care: Seeking medical or psychological help, Avoid Emotional Stress: Situations that make me feel strong emotions, Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

When Asha was detained during a visit to her home country two years ago, the worst moments came in a small concrete room with no windows and a heavy metal door that shut with a sound she still hears in her body. She was interrogated for hours, not knowing when anyone would come in, and she learned quickly that safety depended on staying alert to tiny signs: footsteps in the corridor, the scrape of a chair, the angle of the door, where the exit was and whether anyone was blocking it. She was threatened, restrained, and repeatedly made to feel that her body and fear no longer belonged to her. What stayed with her afterward was not only the memory of what was done to her, but the conviction that danger arrives without warning and that the only chance of surviving it is to never let herself soften or be caught off guard.

Back in the United States, Asha returned to her life with her husband and to her work as a tailor in a neighborhood alterations shop, but she did not return to feeling ordinary. Almost as soon as she enters any place, her eyes move automatically to the door, then to the back exit, then to who is standing near them. At the shop she notices every customer who lingers too long and every man whose voice carries across the room. The hum of the iron, the click of scissors, even the curtain of a fitting room shifting can make her body tense before she has time to think. She describes living “like a wire pulled tight,” always watching, always braced.

At times the past does not feel past. If she hears pounding footsteps in the hallway behind the shop or a heavy door slam in the building, she can suddenly feel as if she is back in that room, her heart racing and her body preparing for something terrible to happen. In those moments she is not simply remembering; she is there again, frozen and flooded, scanning the space as if someone might enter at any second. Because these episodes come on so quickly, what frightens her most is the sense that she can lose the present without warning. That constant watchfulness and the shock of being thrown back into the torture have gradually shaped how she lives now: she avoids anything that might lower her guard or stir up the feelings she works so hard to contain.

She has stopped going to doctors unless her husband insists, and even then she has canceled appointments at the last minute. Sitting in an exam room with the door closed feels intolerable; she is certain she will be trapped, watched, or touched when she cannot control what happens next. The same fear has kept her from seeking psychological help until now. She says that talking in detail about what happened feels too risky, as though letting herself feel it fully might make the memories take over. When her husband tries to encourage her to “open up,” she changes the subject or leaves the room because strong emotion feels like the beginning of losing control.

The pattern has spread into the smallest parts of her day. At work, when business is slow and her coworkers chat over tea, Asha keeps her hands busy with hemming or rethreading machines rather than sitting still. Relaxing feels dangerous to her, not comforting; if she leans back, closes her eyes, or lets her mind drift, she expects she will miss something important and be caught defenseless. Even at home she chooses the chair with the clearest view of the apartment door and startles if her husband walks in unexpectedly. He has come to see how hard she works to stay composed, but he also feels shut out by it. Their evenings, once quiet and companionable, are now organized around avoiding whatever might upset her.

Over months this has narrowed her life. She takes fewer clients because unexpected fittings with unfamiliar men make her too tense, and she no longer accompanies her husband to family gatherings where she would have to sit in crowded rooms without a clear exit. The more she avoids medical offices, emotionally charged conversations, and even moments of rest, the more foreign and uncontrollable the flashbacks seem when they do break through. She has come to believe that vigilance is the only thing keeping her safe, so any loosening of it feels reckless.

Asha finally sought help after ducking to the floor at the shop when a deliveryman slammed the back door, then finding herself unable to stop shaking while a customer stared. She was ashamed, but more than that she was frightened by how completely the past could overtake her in the middle of an ordinary workday. She says she wants her life back with her husband and wants to be able to sit still without feeling endangered, but she is deeply afraid that if she lets herself speak about what happened, she will be pulled fully back into it and not find her way out.
